title: Phase Transition from Random Features to Fully Trainable Networks
tldr: This paper quantifies a phase transition in neural network approximation bounds when transitioning from fixed random features to trainable parameters. The research reveals that training as few as 4.1% of parameters captures 90% of performance gains over fixed representations.
takeaways: Establishes a squared L2 approximation rate of O((k_P log(m/delta)/m)^alpha) for width-m networks with trainable proportion P.
Proves that in 5D biased-ReLU networks, a 4.1% trainable parameter proportion achieves 90% of total theoretical error reduction.
Demonstrates empirical phase transitions in training error across multi-layer models up to 15 layers deep.
fullAnalysis:
The authors analyze partially trainable neural networks bridging fixed random feature methods and fully adaptive models. Using leverage compatibility and polynomial spectral decay with exponent alpha > 1, they formalize an L2 approximation rate in a Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS). The derived bound shows that parameter efficiency exhibits diminishing returns after an initial sharp improvement, governed by fixed and trainable sampling mismatch constants k_0* and k_1*.

This framework provides strong theoretical backing for Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) and frozen-backbone architectures. For instance, in spherical biased-ReLU features at dimension d=5 and initialization scale tau=10, a trainable parameter ratio of only ~4.1% recovers 90% of the theoretical approximation gain of a 100% trainable model. Numerical experiments across architectures up to 15 layers confirm that this theoretical phase transition translates directly into actual gradient descent training dynamics.
